chief_complaint: severe ear canal pain, discharge, pain on pulling earlobe
hpi_details: A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic with severe ear canal pain, discharge, pain on pulling earlobe. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks dirty pool water got trapped inside her ear canal or that she scratched the canal wall with a cotton swab.
concerns: She is worried that the severe pain and drainage mean her eardrum has burst and her hearing will be permanently impaired.
expectations: She hopes to have her ear canal cleaned out and to receive prescription antibiotic ear drops for fast pain relief.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Otitis Externa evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Otitis Externa is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes aural toilet (canal cleaning) plus topical Ciprofloxacin-Dexamethasone ear drops, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Key HPI features: A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic with severe ear canal pain, discharge, pain on pulling earlobe. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Otitis Externa.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Otitis Externa.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Otitis media without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe pain out of proportion to exam findings in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient — concerning for malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa.
management_principles: Plan for Acute Otitis Externa: Aural toilet, Ciprofloxacin-Dexamethasone ear drops
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

history.answer: My right ear has been hurting terribly, and there is yellow fluid draining out of it.
It started about three days ago in my right ear, and the pain has been getting steadily worse each day.
It is a severe, constant throbbing pain that I would rate an eight out of ten, and it keeps me awake at night.
Yes, whenever I pull on my earlobe or touch the front of my ear it hurts intensely, and chewing also makes it ache.
history.topic: Pain with ear pulling and chewing

history.answer: There has been a yellowish, watery fluid draining out with a slight odor, but I have not seen any blood.
My right ear feels completely plugged and muffled, like it is stuffed with cotton, though my left ear hears normally.
No, I haven't noticed any ringing sounds, and the room is not spinning at all.
I have not measured a fever or had chills, and I haven't had a cough, runny nose, or cold symptoms.
No, both sides of my face move normally, and I haven't seen any blisters around or inside my ear.
No, there is no swelling or redness behind my ear, and I do not have a stiff neck or bad headache.
I went swimming at a community pool four days ago, and I used cotton swabs afterward to clean and dry inside my ear.
Yes, right before the pain became severe, the inside of my ear canal was itching like crazy.
No, I haven't been hit on the ear, heard any loud explosions, or felt any bug crawl inside.
No, I have not traveled by airplane or done any scuba diving recently.
My teeth feel fine, and my jaw joint doesn't click or hurt by itself, only when chewing pulls near the ear canal.
No, my throat feels fine, swallowing is normal, my voice is not hoarse, and I don't feel any lumps in my neck.
I had swimmer's ear once many years ago after a vacation, but I have never had chronic middle ear infections, ruptured eardrums, or ear surgery.
No, I have never had diabetes, and I don't have any condition that suppresses my immune system.
I have felt worn out and fatigued over the last couple of days, mainly because the ear pain made it hard to sleep.
I thought some pool water got trapped inside or I scratched the inside of my ear with a cotton swab and infected it.
The pain is so sharp and with this leaking fluid, I'm terrified my eardrum burst and my hearing will be permanently damaged.

I don't have any chronic medical conditions, no high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital stays.

I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.

exam.finding: Alert and oriented female appearing uncomfortable and protective of her right ear, but in no acute cardiopulmonary distress.
Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Severe pain elicited on right tragal pressure and pinna traction; right external auditory canal is markedly erythematous and edematous with yellowish discharge, while the left ear is normal.
Weber test lateralizes to the right ear, and Rinne test shows bone conduction greater than air conduction on the right ear, consistent with conductive hearing loss from canal swelling.
Facial nerve function is intact bilaterally with symmetric forehead wrinkling, eye closure, and smiling, and no vesicles or facial weakness are present.
Tender, mobile right preauricular lymph node palpable, with no mastoid tenderness, erythema, or fluctuance behind the ear.
Temporomandibular joints have normal range of motion without clicking, crepitus, or intrinsic joint tenderness.
Nasal mucosa is normal without congestion; oral cavity and posterior pharynx are clear without erythema or tonsillar swelling.
